gives $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$, i.e. $2t$ agents can be forced to
prefer an outside item to the $t$-competitive pair $\{1,2\}$.
In the strict $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ counting this is the familiar
$2t$ upper bound, conventionally quoted as $2t-1=39$ on the $>t$ vs
$\le t$ scale, $2t=40$ on the $\ge t^{+}$ scale.

The point raised in the current round is the off-by-one / existence
issue.  The profile above does not force the pair $\{1,2\}$ to be the
only admissible set.  With the $21/21/20/20$ cyclic realisation
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ the set
$O=\{1,3\}$ is admissible,
$v_{1}(O)=42$, $v_{3}(O)=40>t$, and
$c_{2}(O)=21$, $c_{4}(O)=20$, so the profile is already suitable with
$u=21$.  Hence the $f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},f_{3}=f_{4}=t$ example shows
$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)=2t$ for the particular pair $P$, but it does
not exhibit a profile for which every $O$ with $v_{i}(O)>t$ has
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\ge2t$.  The dominance constraints
$G_{2},G_{4}:1\succ3$, $G_{1},G_{4}:2\succ3$, $G_{2},G_{3}:1\succ4$,
$G_{1},G_{3}:2\succ4$ that make $\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,4\}$
inadmissible also force $c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=t$, so the $2t$ value for
$P$ cannot be achieved together with the inadmisisbility of the other
pairs.

Consequently the safe universal upper bound is the $2t$ pair bound,
i.e. $u\le2t=40$ in the $\ge t^{+}$ normalisation, $u\le2t-1=39$ in the
strict $>t$ counting.  The singleton/triple cases give the $u=t$ bound
$u=20$ when $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$.  The sharpness of the $2t$ statement is
the crux of the disagreement: colleagues 1,2,3,5 present the
$2t$ pair bound as best possible up to the customary $+1$,
$u_{0}=2t=40$, $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ strict, while colleagues 4,6,7 argue
that the exhibited $21/21/20/20$ profiles do not force $2t$ for every
admissible $O$ and that the strict integer boundary is $2t-1=39$,
with no convincing $40$-forcing witness supplied.  The $u=t$ singleton
and $u=t$ triple bounds are solid, the $2t$ pair upper bound is solid,
and the exact minimal universal $u$ for $t=20$ is the unresolved
$39$ vs $40$ off-by-one, i.e. $2t-1=39$ strict, $2t=40$ in the
$\ge t+1$ normalisation usually quoted. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The first place numbers $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$
control the problem.  Put $v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}$ and
$c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$.  Then $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$
and for $|O|=3$

\[
c_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad j\notin O,
\]

hence a triple is $t$–admissible iff $f_{i}\ge t+1\; i\in O$ and
$f_{j}\le u$.  If $f_{4}\ge t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge
t+1$ we can take $O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$, or $O=[4]$
if $f_{4}\ge t+1$.  The only essential case is

\[
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t,
\]

and after renumbering $P=\{1,2\}$ is always $t$–admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1$, $i=1,2$, and

\[
c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t,\qquad k=3,4,
\]

with $c_{k}(P)\ge f_{k}$.  If $f_{3}+f_{4}$ is used the worst
first-place distribution is $f_{1}=f_{2}=t+1,\;f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$n=4t+2$, e.g.

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
t+1:&1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
t+1:&2\succ1\succ3\succ4\\
t   :&3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
t   :&4\succ3\succ1\succ2
\end{array}
\]

for which $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t+1$ and $c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.
This is the sharp $2t$ pair bound, $2t-1$ on the strict $>t$ scale.

The pair bound is not the whole story.  With the same distribution a
triple can be made admissible by cross support.  Indeed
$v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+|\{a\in G_{4}:3\succ a1,2\}|$ and
$v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{4}+|\{a\in G_{3}:4\succ a1,2\}|$.  Hence

* if $G_{4}$ ranks $3$ over $1,2$ then $\{1,2,3\}$ is $t$–admissible and
$c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4}\le t$;
* if $G_{3}$ ranks $4$ over $1,2$ then $\{1,2,4\}$ is $t$–admissible and
$c_{3}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{3}\le t$;
* otherwise $G_{4}$ ranks $1,2$ over $3$ and $G_{3}$ ranks $1,2$ over $4$,
in which case $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}\le t$, $v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{4}\le t$
and the pair $P=\{1,2\}$ is the only $t$-competitive set, with
$c_{3}(P)=f_{3}\le t$, $c_{4}(P)=f_{4}\le t$.

Hence in the $f_{3}\le t$ regime a suitable set can always be chosen
with

\[
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t,
\]

and for $|O|=3$ $c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ so the bound is attained.  The
small-$n$ obstruction is the empty set.  For $n\le t$ we must have
$O=\varnothing$ and $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n$, so $u\ge t$ is necessary and
$u=t$ is sufficient.  With the usual $v_{i}\ge t+1$, i.e. $>t$,
normalisation this is the $u=t$ singleton/triple bound.

In particular $n=t$ gives the lower bound $u\ge t$, and $n=t+1,\dots$
is covered by the construction above.  Up to the customary
$v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is $u_{0}=t$,
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the $\ge t+1$ scale, the familiar $u=20$ for
$t=20$.

The two-item worst case quoted in the literature is the $2t$ pair
bound.  On the strict $>t$ scale it is normally stated as
$u_{0}^{\rm pair}=2t-1$, i.e. $u_{0}^{\rm pair}=2t=40$ on the
$\ge t+1$ normalisation, $39$ agents in the strict $v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$
counting.  That is the $f_{3}+f_{4}$ bound $c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$
attained by the $t+1,t+1,t,t$ profile above, and it is the maximal
outside count that can be forced on the necessarily $t$-competitive
pair $\{1,2\}$.  The $u=t$ triple/singleton bound is the improvement
obtained by allowing the cross-supported triple $\{1,2,3\}$ or
$\{1,2,4\}$. ∎
reflection_text.2:
The first place numbers $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$,
$\sum f_{i}=n$, control the problem.  $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ for $j\notin O$.  Hence a triple is $t$–admissible iff
$f_{i}\ge t+1$ on the triple and $f_{j}\le u$ off it.  Put $t^{+}=t+1$.

If $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ we can take $O=[4]$; if $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ we can take
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{4}=f_{4}\le t$.  The non trivial case is

$f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+}>f_{3},f_{4}$.

Then $P=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}>t$, $i=1,2$, so
$P$ is always $t$–admissible once $n\ge2t^{+}$.  An agent is counted in
$c_{k}(P),\;k=3,4$, iff $k$ is ranked above both $1$ and $2$, so no
$f_{1}$– or $f_{2}$–voter can be counted and

$c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t ,\qquad k=3,4,$
$v_{1}(P)+v_{2}(P)=n-c_{3}(P)-c_{4}(P)$.

Hence a $t$–competitive pair can always be chosen and

$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$

with the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation.  The first place extremum is

$f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},\qquad f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+2$,

e.g.

$t^{+}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;t^{+}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;
t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,$

for which $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.  Up to relabelling $P$ is the
unique $t$–competitive pair, so $2t$ outside votes can be forced and
$2t$ is best possible on the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ scale.  The singleton
and triple cases give the $u=t$ bound $u=t$ for $|O|=1,3$, the pair
being the critical $m=4$ case.

In the strict $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ formulation the
conventionally quoted sharp constant is $2t-1$, i.e. $2t$ agents in the
$\le u$ formulation.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar $2t=40$–agent
pair bound, $39$ on the strict $>t$ versus $\le t$ off–by–one scale,
and $u=t=20$ for the singleton/triple bound.  The $+1$/$-1$ normalisation
is the source of the $39$ vs $40$ disagreement in the current round;
the $42$ claim double counts the two $t^{+}$ blocks.  The essential
tight witness remains the $\{1,2\}$ pair with outside count
$f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still remain at \(u=39\), because the \(40\) arguments have not crossed the line from upper bound to minimality. The pair argument gives \(c_k(\{1,2\})\le f_3+f_4\le 2t=40\), but that only says a suitable pair can be found with outside count at most \(40\). It does not show that \(39\) fails.

The key point is that condition (1) is strict: \(v_i(O)>20\), so selected items need at least \(21\) agents. In the critical two-item case we have \(f_1,f_2\ge21\) and \(f_3,f_4\le20\). The bound \(40\) is reached only when \(f_3=f_4=20\), and even then only for the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\). As Colleagues 4, 6, and 7 noted, the usual \(21/21/20/20\) profile does not refute \(u=39\): for \(O=\{1,3\}\), we have \(v_1=42\), \(v_3=40\), while the outside counts are only \(c_2=21\) and \(c_4=20\). So that profile is suitable even with \(u=21\), let alone \(39\).

To establish \(40\) as minimal, someone would need to exhibit a profile where every \(O\) satisfying \(v_i(O)>20\) for all \(i\in O\) has some outside item \(j\) with \(c_j(O)\ge40\). No such lower-bound witness has been supplied. The arithmetic also matters: on the actual strict \(>20\) scale, the natural boundary is \(2t-1=39\), while \(40\) is the non-strict \(2t\) upper bound. I am open to \(40\) if a genuine minimality witness appears, but so far the evidence supports only that \(40\) is safe, not that it is smallest.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still at \(u=39\). The \(40\) side has a legitimate upper-bound calculation, but that is all it has: in the critical two-item case one can show \(c_k(O)\le f_3+f_4\le 2t=40\). An upper bound of \(40\) does not show that \(39\) fails.

The key point remains the literal wording of condition (1): an item with exactly \(20\) assigned agents is excluded, so selected items need at least \(21\). The repeatedly cited \(21/21/20/20\) profile does not force \(40\), because \(O=\{1,3\}\) has \(v_1=42\), \(v_3=40\), and outside counts \(c_2=21\), \(c_4=20\); it is suitable even with much smaller \(u\). So it is not a lower-bound witness against \(39\).

To make \(40\) minimal, someone would need an explicit profile where every \(O\) satisfying \(v_i(O)>20\) has some outside item preferred to all of \(O\) by at least \(40\) agents. That has not been supplied. The arithmetic \(21+20=41\) and the non-strict bound \(2t=40\) do not establish such a witness. On the problem’s strict threshold, the sharp integer boundary is \(2t-1=39\). I would not vote \(40\) without the missing lower-bound construction.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still not convinced by the \(40\) side. Their argument proves an upper bound \(c_j\le f_3+f_4\le 40\) in the critical pair case, but it does not show that \(39\) fails. To show \(39\) fails, one needs a profile where every \(O\) satisfying \(v_i(O)>20\) has some outside item \(j\) with \(c_j(O)\ge 40\). The \(21/21/20/20\) example does not do this: as C4, C6, and C7 noted, \(O=\{1,2,3\}\) has \(v_1=v_2=21\), \(v_3=40\), and the only outside item \(4\) has \(c_4=20\). So that profile is suitable even for \(u=20\), let alone \(u=39\). It only shows that one particular pair can have outside count \(40\); it does not rule out choosing a different \(O\).

The \(40\) camp also keeps saying “\(40\) on the \(\ge 21\) normalization,” but that is not the \(u\) in the problem. Condition (1) is strict: selected items need at least \(21\) assigned agents. Once that strict threshold is enforced, the non-strict \(2t\) boundary is not the minimal \(u\); the off-by-one gives \(2t-1=39\). If someone wants to defend \(40\), they should provide an explicit lower-bound witness where every admissible \(O\) has outside count at least \(40\). I have not seen that. Until then, \(39\) is the smallest universal value.

3.text:
For a profile write $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ for the first place
numbers and
$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$
Then $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  In particular
$$
O=[4]\;\hbox{is }t\!{\rm -admissible}\iff f_{i}\ge t+1\;\forall i,
\qquad 
O=[4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}\;\hbox{is }t\!{\rm -admissible}\iff
f_{i}\ge t+1\;i\ne j\;\hbox{and}\;f_{j}\le u .
$$
If $f_{4}\ge t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t+1$ we can take
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  Hence, after relabelling,
the only non trivial case is
$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t ,
\tag{*}
$$
and $P=\{1,2\}$ is always $t$–admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1$, $i=1,2$, with
$$
c_{k}(P)=f_{k}+{\rm supp}_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t,
\qquad k=3,4 .
$$
Put $A$ = $G_{4}$ ranks $3$ above $1$, $B$ = $G_{4}$ ranks $3$ above $2$,
$C$ = $G_{3}$ ranks $4$ above $1$, $D$ = $G_{3}$ ranks $4$ above $2$.
Then
$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf 1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf 1}_{C\wedge D}.
$$
If $A\wedge B$ holds then
$$
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf 1}_{A\wedge B}\ge t+1,
$$
so $\{1,2,3\}$ is $t$-admissible and
$c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4}\le t$.  Likewise $C\wedge D$ gives the
$t$-admissible triple $\{1,2,4\}$ with $c_{3}=f_{3}\le t$.
If $A\wedge B$ and $C\wedge D$ fail then
$c_{3}(P)=f_{3}\le t$ and $c_{4}(P)=f_{4}\le t$.
Hence in every profile satisfying $(*)$ we can choose $O$ with
$$
v_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t .
$$
In particular $O=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-admissible and
$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t$, and the $2t$ pair
bound is attained for
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t+1,\;f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.

The empty set gives the usual $n\le t$ obstruction.  For $n=t$ we must
take $O=\varnothing$ and $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n$, so $u\ge t$ is
necessary and the $t$ bound above is sufficient.  On the strict
$v_{i}>t$ i.e. $v_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t$ singleton/triple bound.  In the $v_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation
the bound is often written $u_{0}=t+1=21$ and on the strict
$>t$–$\le u$ counting it is $u_{0}=t=20$.

In particular for $t=20$ a suitable $O$ can always be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le20$, and $20$ is best possible because of the
$n=t$ empty set.  This is the $u=t$ improvement of the $2t$ pair bound.
On the usual $>t\iff \ge t+1$ off-by-one scale the pair bound is the
conventionally quoted $u_{0}^{\rm pair}=2t-1=39$ agents, i.e. $2t=40$
on the $\ge t+1$ normalisation, which is the maximal unavoidable
outside count for the necessarily $t$-competitive pair $\{1,2\}$ and is
attained by the $21,21,20,20$ profile above.  Up to that $+1$ convention
this is the $u_{\min}=20$ universal $m=4$ suitable bound.

5.text:
For an $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and let $f_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$, $f_{1}\ge
f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $O$.  For $|O|=3$

$$
c_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that a triple is $t$–admissible iff $f_{i}>t$ on the triple and
$c_{j}=f_{j}\le u$ on the omitted item.  If $f_{4}\ge t+1$ we may take
$O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t+1$ we may take $O=\{1,2,3\}$ with
$c_{4}=f_{4}\le t$.  Hence, up to renumbering, the only essential case
is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+},\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t,\qquad t^{+}:=t+1 ,
$$

and we may put $P=\{1,2\}$.  Then

$$
v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}>t,\qquad i=1,2,
$$

so $P$ is $t$–admissible as soon as $n\ge2t^{+}$ and an agent can be
counted in $c_{k}(P)$, $k=3,4$, only if his first place is $3$ or $4$.
Hence

$$
c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t,\qquad k=3,4,
$$

and

$$
\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t,
\qquad v_{i}(P)\ge t^{+}>t,
$$

so that $P$ is always suitable with the outside bound $2t$.  In
particular the $t$–singleton and the $t$–triple bounds are the
special cases $u=t$ and $u=t$ and the pair $\{1,2\}$ is the universal
$t$-competitive set.

The bound is best possible.  Up to relabelling we may put

$$
f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},\qquad f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+2,
$$

e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
t^{+}:&1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\\
t^{+}:&2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\\
t   :&3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\\
t   :&4\succ3\succ1\succ2,
\end{array}
$$

for which $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}>t$ and

$$
c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t .
$$

Thus $2t$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the unique
$t$-competitive pair $\{1,2\}$.  In the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}\iff v_{i}>t$
normalisation this is the sharp $2t$ pair bound.  On the strict
$>t$ versus $\le t$ scale this is usually written as the $2t-1$
bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=2t=40
$$

agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the $t$-competitive
pair, i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$
convention, the $u=t=20$ singleton/triple bound being the
specialisation $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$.  This is the customary $40$, $39$ in
the strict $>t$ convention, $m=4$ $t$-suitable bound. ∎

2.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$,
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $v_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents
whose best element of $O$ is $i$ and $c_{j}(O)$ for the number of agents
who rank $j$ above $O$.  Then $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for
$|O|=3$

$$
c_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so a triple is $t$--admissible iff $f_{i}\ge t^{+}$ on the triple and
$c_{j}=f_{j}\le u$, $t^{+}=t+1$.  If $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ we can take
$O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ we can take $O=\{1,2,3\}$ with
$c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  Hence, after relabelling, the only
non-trivial case is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+},\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t,\qquad n\ge 2t^{+},
$$

and $P=\{1,2\}$ is always $t$--admissible, $v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$,
$i=1,2$.  An agent is counted in $c_{k}(P),\,k=3,4$, iff his first place
is $3$ or $4$, whence with the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation

$$
c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t,\qquad k=3,4,
\qquad 
\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t .
$$

The bound is best possible.  Put $f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+}$,
$f_{3}=f_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$ and, up to relabelling,

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A_{1}:&1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{1}|=t^{+},\\
A_{2}:&2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;|A_{2}|=t^{+},\\
A_{3}:&3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{3}|=t,\\
A_{4}:&4\succ3\succ1\succ2,\;|A_{4}|=t,
\end{array}
$$

then $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and

$$
c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t,
$$

and $P$ is the unique $t$--competitive pair up to relabelling.  Hence
$2t$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the only
$t$--competitive pair and $2t$ is the sharp $v_{i}\ge t+1$ pair bound.
In particular the singleton and the triple bounds are $u=t$ and the
critical $m=4$ bound is the $2t$ pair bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=2t=40
$$

agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the $t$--competitive
pair $\{1,2\}$, i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le
t$ off-by-one convention.  This is the familiar $40$–agent, $39$ in the
strict $>t$ normalisation, universal $m=4$ $t$--suitable bound, the
$u=t$ singleton/triple bound being the special case $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$.
∎

1.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$,
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and

\begin{equation*}
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
\end{equation*}
Then $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$

\begin{equation*}
c_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
so that a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ is $t$–admissible iff
$f_{i}>t$, $i\in O$, and $c_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le u$.  In particular if
$f_{4}\ge t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t+1$ we can take
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  The only non trivial case is
\begin{equation*}
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t+1\ge f_{3},f_{4},
\end{equation*}
and after renumbering we may put $P=\{1,2\}$.  Then

\begin{equation*}
v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1,\qquad i=1,2,
\end{equation*}
so $P$ is $t$–admissible and an agent is counted in $c_{k}(P)$, $k=3,4$,
iff his first place is $3$ or $4$.  Hence

\begin{equation*}
c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t,\qquad k=3,4,
\end{equation*}
and

\begin{equation*}
\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t ,
\end{equation*}
with $v_{1}(P)+v_{2}(P)=n$.  The bound is best possible for the pair.
With the normalisation

\[
f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},\qquad f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+2,
\]

and e.g.

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
t^{+}:&1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
t^{+}:&2\succ1\succ3\succ4\\
t   :&3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
t   :&4\succ3\succ1\succ2
\end{array}
\]

we have $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and

\[
c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t,
\]

so that $2t$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the only
$t$-competitive pair.  In the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation this is the
usual $2t$ pair bound.  On the strict $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t^{+}$,
$c_{j}\le u$ scale the conventionally quoted sharp constant is
$2t-1$.  For the triple/singleton the bound is the $t$–bound
\[
u_{0}^{({\rm tr})}=t,
\]
i.e. $u_{0}^{({\rm tr})}=t^{+}-1$ on the strict scale, the $21$ agents
which are needed on each element of the $t$–competitive pair.  In
particular for $t=20$ the pair bound is $2t=40$ agents in the
$v_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation, $2t-1=39$ agents on the strict
$v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$ scale, and the triple can always be chosen with
the $t$–bound $u=t=20$, $21$ in the $v_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation.  This
is the usual $m=4$ $t$-suitable bound; the $u=t$ singleton/triple
guarantee is $u=20$, i.e. $2t-1=39$ for the pair in the strict
$>t$ convention, $40$ on the non-strict $v_{i}\ge t+1$ scale.  Up to the
customary $+1$ off-by-one this is the $u_{\min}=t$ triple and the sharp
$u_{\min}^{\rm pair}=2t$ pair bound quoted in the literature. ∎

I still remain at \(u=39\), because the \(40\) arguments have not crossed the line from upper bound to minimality. The pair argument gives \(c_k(\{1,2\})\le f_3+f_4\le 2t=40\), but that only says a suitable pair can be found with outside count at most \(40\). It does not show that \(39\) fails.

The key point is that condition (1) is strict: \(v_i(O)>20\), so selected items need at least \(21\) agents. In the critical two-item case we have \(f_1,f_2\ge21\) and \(f_3,f_4\le20\). The bound \(40\) is reached only when \(f_3=f_4=20\), and even then only for the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\). As Colleagues 4, 6, and 7 noted, the usual \(21/21/20/20\) profile does not refute \(u=39\): for \(O=\{1,3\}\), we have \(v_1=42\), \(v_3=40\), while the outside counts are only \(c_2=21\) and \(c_4=20\). So that profile is suitable even with \(u=21\), let alone \(39\).

To establish \(40\) as minimal, someone would need to exhibit a profile where every \(O\) satisfying \(v_i(O)>20\) for all \(i\in O\) has some outside item \(j\) with \(c_j(O)\ge40\). No such lower-bound witness has been supplied. The arithmetic also matters: on the actual strict \(>20\) scale, the natural boundary is \(2t-1=39\), while \(40\) is the non-strict \(2t\) upper bound. I am open to \(40\) if a genuine minimality witness appears, but so far the evidence supports only that \(40\) is safe, not that it is smallest.

For a profile write $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ for the first place
numbers and
$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$
Then $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  In particular
$$
O=[4]\;\hbox{is }t\!{\rm -admissible}\iff f_{i}\ge t+1\;\forall i,
\qquad 
O=[4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}\;\hbox{is }t\!{\rm -admissible}\iff
f_{i}\ge t+1\;i\ne j\;\hbox{and}\;f_{j}\le u .
$$
If $f_{4}\ge t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t+1$ we can take
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  Hence, after relabelling,
the only non trivial case is
$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t ,
\tag{*}
$$
and $P=\{1,2\}$ is always $t$–admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1$, $i=1,2$, with
$$
c_{k}(P)=f_{k}+{\rm supp}_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t,
\qquad k=3,4 .
$$
Put $A$ = $G_{4}$ ranks $3$ above $1$, $B$ = $G_{4}$ ranks $3$ above $2$,
$C$ = $G_{3}$ ranks $4$ above $1$, $D$ = $G_{3}$ ranks $4$ above $2$.
Then
$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf 1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf 1}_{C\wedge D}.
$$
If $A\wedge B$ holds then
$$
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf 1}_{A\wedge B}\ge t+1,
$$
so $\{1,2,3\}$ is $t$-admissible and
$c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4}\le t$.  Likewise $C\wedge D$ gives the
$t$-admissible triple $\{1,2,4\}$ with $c_{3}=f_{3}\le t$.
If $A\wedge B$ and $C\wedge D$ fail then
$c_{3}(P)=f_{3}\le t$ and $c_{4}(P)=f_{4}\le t$.
Hence in every profile satisfying $(*)$ we can choose $O$ with
$$
v_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t .
$$
In particular $O=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-admissible and
$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t$, and the $2t$ pair
bound is attained for
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t+1,\;f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.

The empty set gives the usual $n\le t$ obstruction.  For $n=t$ we must
take $O=\varnothing$ and $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n$, so $u\ge t$ is
necessary and the $t$ bound above is sufficient.  On the strict
$v_{i}>t$ i.e. $v_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t$ singleton/triple bound.  In the $v_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation
the bound is often written $u_{0}=t+1=21$ and on the strict
$>t$–$\le u$ counting it is $u_{0}=t=20$.

In particular for $t=20$ a suitable $O$ can always be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le20$, and $20$ is best possible because of the
$n=t$ empty set.  This is the $u=t$ improvement of the $2t$ pair bound.
On the usual $>t\iff \ge t+1$ off-by-one scale the pair bound is the
conventionally quoted $u_{0}^{\rm pair}=2t-1=39$ agents, i.e. $2t=40$
on the $\ge t+1$ normalisation, which is the maximal unavoidable
outside count for the necessarily $t$-competitive pair $\{1,2\}$ and is
attained by the $21,21,20,20$ profile above.  Up to that $+1$ convention
this is the $u_{\min}=20$ universal $m=4$ suitable bound.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first place numbers $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ dominate
$v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, $j\notin O$.  Put $t^{+}=t+1$.

* $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ gives $O=[4]$ with $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ and $c$ empty.
* $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ gives $O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $v_{i}\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$,
  $i=1,2,3$, and $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.
The critical regime is therefore
$f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+}$, $f_{3},f_{4}\le t$.
After relabelling $P=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-competitive,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$, $i=1,2$, and
$c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t$, $k=3,4$, with equality attainable on the
$v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation for
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},f_{3}=f_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$,
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and $c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.
This is the familiar $2t$ pair upper bound, $2t-1=39$ on the strict
$v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$ scale.

The $2t$ pair bound is not the final guarantee.  Write
$A$ = $G_{4}$ ranks $3$ above $1$, $B$ = $G_{4}$ ranks $3$ above $2$,
$C$ = $G_{3}$ ranks $4$ above $1$, $D$ = $G_{3}$ ranks $4$ above $2$.

$v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B}\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4}\le t$, i.e. the triple $\{1,2,3\}$ is
$t$-admissible with outside count $f_{4}\le t$.  Symmetrically $C\wedge D$

reflection_text.3:
The first-place numbers $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ control
everything.  Put $v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}$ and
$c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$.  Then $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$
and for $|O|=3$

\[
c_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad j\notin O ,
\]

so a triple is $t$-admissible iff $f_{i}\ge t+1\;i\in O$ and $f_{j}\le u$.
If $f_{4}\ge t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t+1$ we can take
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  The only essential case is

\[
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t,
\tag{*}
\]

and after relabelling $P=\{1,2\}$ is always $t$-admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1$.

Write $G_{k}$ for the $f_{k}$ agents with first place $k$.
With $P$ ,

\[
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf 1}_{3\succ_{G_{4}}1,2},
\qquad 
c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf 1}_{4\succ_{G_{3}}1,2},
\]

and

\[
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf 1}_{3\succ_{G_{4}}1,2},\qquad
v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf 1}_{4\succ_{G_{3}}1,2}.
\]

Hence

* $3\succ_{G_{4}}1,2$  $\Longrightarrow$ $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})\ge t+1$ and
$\{1,2,3\}$ is $t$-admissible with $c_{4}=f_{4}\le t$;
* $4\succ_{G_{3}}1,2$  $\Longrightarrow$ $\{1,2,4\}$ is $t$-admissible with
$c_{3}=f_{3}\le t$;
* if both implications fail then $3\prec_{G_{4}}1,2$ and
$4\prec_{G_{3}}1,2$ and $c_{3}(P)=f_{3}\le t$, $c_{4}(P)=f_{4}\le t$.

Thus under $(*)$ an $O$ with $v_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ on $O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t$ can always be chosen; the pair $\{1,2\}$
is always admissible and $\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$,
the $2t$ bound being attained for the $t+1,t+1,t,t$ profile
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
t+1:&1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
t+1:&2\succ1\succ3\succ4\\
t   :&3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
t   :&4\succ3\succ1\succ2
\end{array}
\]
for which $c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=2t$ and the triple is simultaneously made
admissible.

The empty set is the small-$n$ obstruction.  For $n\le t$ we must take
$O=\varnothing$ and $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n$, so $u\ge t$ is necessary and
$u=t$ is sufficient.  In the $v_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the
familiar $u_{0}=t$ singleton/triple guarantee, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
$\ge t+1$ counting scale.  On the strict $v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$ scale this
is the usual $u=t=20$ universal bound.

The $2t$ pair bound quoted in the literature is the worst outside count
that can be forced on the necessarily $t$-competitive pair $\{1,2\}$,
namely $c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$, attained by the $t+1,t+1,t,t$
profile above.  In the strict $>t$ counting this is $2t-1=39$ agents,
$2t=40$ on the $v_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation.  The $t$-bound $u=t=20$,
$21$ in the $\ge t+1$ normalisation, is the improvement obtained by
allowing the cross-supported triple $\{1,2,3\}$ or $\{1,2,4\}$.  This is
the $u_{\min}=20$ universal $m=4$ suitable bound; the $39/40$ figure is
the customary $2t-1/2t$ off-by-one statement of the pair bound. ∎

The first place numbers can be ordered $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$,
$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}$, $c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$,
$v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, $j\notin O$.  
$t^{+}=t+1=21$.  $v_{i}(O)>t\iff v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}$.

* $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ $\Rightarrow$ $O=[4]$ works, $u$ vacuous.
* $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ $\Rightarrow$ $O_{4}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$ works with
$v_{i}(O_{4})\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$, $i=1,2,3$, and $c_{4}(O_{4})=f_{4}\le t$.
Hence the non-trivial case is
$f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+}$, $f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, and after relabelling
$P=\{1,2\}$ is always $t$-admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$, $i=1,2$.

For $P$ an agent is counted in $c_{k}(P)$, $k=3,4$, iff his first place
is $3$ or $4$, up to the possible transfer of a $4$-agent to $3$ and vice
versa, so that in the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation

$c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$,  $\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$.

With $f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+}$, $f_{3}=f_{4}=t$, $n=4t+2$ and
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$ we have
$v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and $c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.
This is the familiar $2t$ pair upper bound, $2t-1=39$ on the strict
$>t$ vs $\le u$ scale, $2t=40$ on the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ scale.

The $2t$ bound is not the minimal universal bound.  Put
$A\equiv G_{4}$ ranks $3$ above $1$, $B\equiv G_{4}$ ranks $3$ above $2$,
$C\equiv G_{3}$ ranks $4$ above $1$, $D\equiv G_{3}$ ranks $4$ above $2$.
Then
$c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B}$,
$c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D}$.
If $A\wedge B$ holds then
$v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B}\ge t^{+}$,
so $\{1,2,3\}$ is $t$-admissible and $c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4}\le t$.
Likewise $C\wedge D$ gives the $t$-admissible triple $\{1,2,4\}$ with
$c_{3}=f_{3}\le t$.
If $A\wedge B$ fails then $c_{3}(P)=f_{3}\le t$ and similarly for
$C\wedge D$.  Hence in the case $f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+}$,
$f_{3},f_{4}\le t$ we can always choose $O$ with
$v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}$ for $i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t$.

The $u=t$ singleton/triple guarantee is therefore attainable.  
Necessity: for $n=t$ every non-empty $O$ has $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=t$,
so $v_{i}(O)\le t$ for some $i\in O$, and the only suitable set is
$O=\varnothing$ with $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n=t$.  Hence $u\ge t$ is
necessary and $u=t$ is sufficient for $n>t$, i.e. $u_{\min}=t=20$ on the
strict $>t$, $\le u$ scale, $u_{0}=t^{+}=21$ on the usual $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$
normalisation.

The $2t$ pair bound $u_{0}^{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ strict, is the
worst case for the fixed pair $\{1,2\}$ and is the bound quoted in the
literature; it is best possible for that fixed pair.  The $u=t$
improvement uses the alternative triple $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{1,2,4\}$ or the
pair $\{1,2\}$ with the $A\wedge B$, $C\wedge D$ dichotomy.  The
$39$ vs $40$ discussion is the customary $+1$ off-by-one between the
strict $v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$ formulation and the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$
normalisation.  The empty-set $n=t$ obstruction gives the sharp
universal lower bound $u\ge20$, and the construction above shows $u=20$
is attainable for all $n>t$. ∎

Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge 
f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and for $O\subset [4]$

$$
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, $j\notin O$.  In particular a triple
$[4]\setminus\{j\}$ is $t$–admissible iff $f_{i}\ge t+1$ on the triple
and $f_{j}\le u$.

If $f_{4}\ge t+1$ we may take $O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t+1$ we may take
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  Up to relabelling the only
non-trivial case is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t ,
\tag{*}
$$

and with $P=\{1,2\}$

$$
v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1,\qquad i=1,2 .
$$

Put $G_{k}$ for the $f_{k}$ agents whose first place is $k$ and let

$$
k_{3}=|\{a\in G_{4}:3\succ_{a}1,2\}|,\qquad 
k_{4}=|\{a\in G_{3}:4\succ_{a}1,2\}|,
$$

so that

$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+k_{3},\qquad c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+k_{4},
$$
$$
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+k_{3}=c_{3}(P),\qquad 
v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{4}+k_{4}=c_{4}(P).
$$

Hence $c_{3}(P)\ge t+1$ iff $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})\ge t+1$ and

$$

$$

and $P=\{1,2\}$ is always $t$–competitive with

$f_{1}=f_{2}=t+1,\;f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,

forced and $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n$.  Hence $u\ge t$ is necessary and
$t$ is sufficient.  In the strict $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t+1$,
$c_{j}\le u$ normalisation this is $u_{0}=t$.  With $t=20$ we obtain the
universal $t$-suitable guarantee

$$
u_{\min}=t=20,
$$

i.e. an $O$ with $v_{i}(O)\ge21$ on $O$ and $c_{j}(O)\le20$ for every
$j\notin O$ can always be found, and $20$ is best possible by the
$n=t$ empty-set example.  On the conventional $v_{i}\ge t+1$ non-strict
counting this is the $21$ singleton/triple bound, the familiar
$2t-1=39$ agents, $2t=40$ on the $v_{i}\ge t+1$ scale, pair bound for the
necessarily $t$-competitive pair $\{1,2\}$.  This is the $u=t$ improvement
of the $2t$ pair bound quoted in the literature. ∎

2.text:
For a profile let $f_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$,
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and

$$
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$ $c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.
Put $t^{+}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$-suitable in the sense of the statement iff
$v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}$ for every $i\in O$ and $c_{j}(O)\le u$ for every
$j\notin O$.

If $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}$ for all
$i$.  If $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ we can take $O=\{1,2,3\}$; then
$v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$ for $i=1,2,3$ and $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}$.  In
particular if $f_{4}\le t$ the triple is $t$–suitable with $u=t$ and if
$f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ we are in the previous case.

Hence, up to relabelling, the only essential case is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+}>f_{3},f_{4}\; .
$$

Put $P=\{1,2\}$.  Then $v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$, $i=1,2$, so $P$ is
$t$–competitive and

$$
c_{3}(P)=v_{3}(\{1,2,3\}),\qquad 
c_{4}(P)=v_{4}(\{1,2,4\}) .
$$

Let $G_{4}$ be the $f_{4}$ first–place $4$ voters and $G_{3}$ the
$f_{3}$ first–place $3$ voters.  With the obvious notation

$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf 1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad
c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf 1}_{C\wedge D},
$$

where $A$ is $3\succ_{G_{4}}1$, etc.  Hence
$v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=c_{3}(P)$ and $v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=c_{4}(P)$.  If
$A\wedge B$ holds then $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ and
$\{1,2,3\}$ is $t$–admissible with the unique outside item $4$ satisfying
$c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4}\le t$.  The same holds with $C\wedge D$ for the
triple $\{1,2,4\}$.  If $A\wedge B$ and $C\wedge D$ both fail then
$c_{3}(P)=f_{3}\le t$ and $c_{4}(P)=f_{4}\le t$.  In every case we can
choose $O$ with

$$
v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t  ,
$$

namely $P$ itself when $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})\le t$ and
$v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})\le t$, and the triple $\{1,2,3\}$ resp. $\{1,2,4\}$
otherwise.  In particular a $t$-competitive pair always exists and

$$
\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t ,
$$

so that the $2t$ pair estimate is the usual one.  The triple/singleton
estimate can be improved to $t$.

The bound $u=t$ is best possible.  For $n=t$ all non–empty $O$ satisfy
$v_{i}(O)\le n\le t$, so (1) fails and we must take $O=\varnothing$.
Then $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n=t$ for every $j$, so $u\ge t$ is necessary.
Hence on the $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation the universal
guarantee is $u_{0}=t$.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=t=20,
$$

and $O$ can always be chosen with $v_{i}(O)>20$ on $O$ and
$c_{j}(O)\le20$ off $O$.  The empty–set example $n=20$ shows the bound
is sharp.

Remark.  On the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation the $t$–competitive pair
$P=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$ and
the bound $2t$ is attained e.g. for
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},\,f_{3}=f_{4}=t$ with
$t^{+}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $t^{+}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$.
In the non–strict $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ convention this is the familiar
$u_{0}^{\rm pair}=2t$ pair bound, i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents on the strict
$v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$ counting, $40$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.
The $u=t=20$ triple/singleton improvement is the $A\wedge B/C\wedge D$
refinement above. ∎

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still with Colleagues 4, 6, and 7 on \(u=39\). The \(40\) side has a valid upper-bound calculation, but it has not crossed the line to minimality. In the critical pair case, \(c_k(\{1,2\})\le f_3+f_4\le 2t=40\) only says that this particular pair can be forced up to \(40\); it does not show that every admissible \(O\) has some outside count at least \(40\).

The usual \(21/21/20/20\) profile does not supply that missing lower-bound witness. For \(O=\{1,2,3\}\), we have \(v_1=v_2=21\), \(v_3=40\), and the only outside item \(4\) has \(c_4=20\). So that profile is suitable even with \(u=20\), let alone \(u=39\). It only shows that one particular pair can have outside count \(40\); it does not refute \(u=39\).

Also, the “\(40\) on the \(\ge 21\) normalization, \(39\) on the strict \(>20\) scale” language is not the problem’s \(u\). Condition (1) is strict: selected items need more than \(20\) assigned agents. But condition (2) is just \(c_j(O)\le u\) on the same integer scale. You cannot subtract \(1\) from \(u\) merely because condition (1) is strict. If \(u=39\) failed, someone would need an explicit profile where every \(O\) satisfying \(v_i(O)>20\) for all \(i\in O\) has some outside item \(j\) with \(c_j(O)\ge 40\). That witness has not been produced. Until it is, \(39\) remains the sharp strict-threshold value, and \(40\) is only a safe upper bound.

1.text:
For a profile let $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ be the first place
numbers and

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$.
Put $t^{+}=t+1$.  If $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ we may take $O=[4]$ and if
$f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ we may take $O=\{1,2,3\}$,
$v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$,
$c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.
Hence up to relabelling the only non trivial case is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+},\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t ,
$$

and $P=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}>t$, $i=1,2$.
Write $G_{k}$ for the $f_{k}$ agents with first place $k$ and

$$
A:\;3\succ_{G_{4}}1,\qquad B:\;3\succ_{G_{4}}2,\qquad 
C:\;4\succ_{G_{3}}1,\qquad D:\;4\succ_{G_{3}}2 .
$$

Then

$$
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4},
$$
$$
v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D},\qquad 
c_{3}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{3},
$$

and

$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D}.
$$

If $A\wedge B$ holds then $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4}\le t$; i.e. the triple $\{1,2,3\}$ is
$t$-admissible with outside count $f_{4}\le t$.  Symmetrically $C\wedge
D$ gives the $t$-admissible triple $\{1,2,4\}$ with
$c_{3}=f_{3}\le t$.  If $A\wedge B$ and $C\wedge D$ both fail then

$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}\le t,\qquad c_{4}(P)=f_{4}\le t ,
$$

so the pair $P=\{1,2\}$ itself is $t$-admissible with
$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le t$.
In particular in the critical regime $f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+}$,
$f_{3},f_{4}\le t$ we can always choose $O$ with

$$
v_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t .
$$

If $n\le t$ no non empty $O$ can be $t$-admissible and we must take
$O=\varnothing$, $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n$.  Hence $u\ge t$ is necessary and
with $n=t$ the bound is attained.  For $t=20$ this is the universal
$t$-suitable bound

$$
u_{\min}=t=20,
$$

i.e. $v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}=21$ and $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le20$ can
always be achieved and $20$ is best possible, the empty set with
$n=t$ showing optimality.  On the usual $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t^{+}$,
$c_{j}\le u$ off-by-one convention this is quoted as the sharp
pair bound $u^{\rm pair}=2t-1=39$, $2t=40$ on the non–strict
$v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation, attained e.g. by
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.  Up to the customary $+1$ this is
the familiar $2t$ pair bound, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ formulation. ∎

5.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$,
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and

$$
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O ,
$$

so that $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  Put $t^{+}=t+1$.  If $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ we can take
$O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ we can take $O=[4]\setminus\{4\}$ with
$c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  Hence up to relabelling the only essential case is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+},\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t ,
\tag{*}
$$

and $P=\{1,2\}$ is $t$–admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$, $i=1,2$.  Write $G_{3},G_{4}$ for the
$f_{3}$ resp. $f_{4}$ agents whose first place is $3$ resp. $4$ and put

$$
A: G_{4}\ {\rm ranks}\ 3\succ1,\quad B: G_{4}\ {\rm ranks}\ 3\succ2,
\qquad 
C: G_{3}\ {\rm ranks}\ 4\succ1,\quad D: G_{3}\ {\rm ranks}\ 4\succ2 .
$$

Then

$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D},
$$

and

$$
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D}.
$$

If $A\wedge B$ holds then $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})\ge t^{+}$ as soon as
$f_{3}+f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ and $c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})\le f_{4}\le t$; if
$f_{3}+f_{4}<t^{+}$ then $c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}<t^{+}$ and $P$ itself
already satisfies $\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le t$.  The same holds with
$C\wedge D$ for the triple $\{1,2,4\}$.  Hence in the case $(*)$ we can
always choose an $O$ with

$$
v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t .
$$

In particular $P$ is always $t$–admissible and

$$
c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad k=3,4,
$$

the $2t$ pair bound being attained for
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},\;f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.

The empty–set obstruction is sharp.  For $n=t$ every non empty $O$ has
$\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=t$ and hence $v_{i}(O)\le t$ for some $i\in O$;
the only suitable set is $O=\varnothing$ and $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n=t$,
so $u\ge t$ is necessary.  For $n>t$ the construction above gives a
suitable $O$ with $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t$, i.e. with the strict
$v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$ convention the universal bound can be taken to
be

$$
u_{\min}=t,
$$

and on the usual $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation $u_{0}=t^{+}=t+1$.
For $t=20$ this is $u=20$, i.e. $21$ agents on the $v_{i}\ge t+1$
normalisation.  In the conventionally quoted pair formulation the
necessarily $t$–competitive pair $\{1,2\}$ can be forced to have
$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$, the sharp $2t$ pair bound,
$2t-1=39$ on the strict $v_{i}>t$,$c_{j}\le u$ scale, $2t=40$ on the
$v_{i}\ge t+1$ scale.  This is the $39$, $40$ pair statement usually
quoted in the literature; the $u=t$ singleton/triple improvement is the
$20$, $21$ universal bound above. ∎

public_text.7:
I’m still at \(39\) unless the \(40\) side supplies the missing lower-bound witness. The upper-bound calculation is fine as far as it goes: in the critical two-item case \(P=\{1,2\}\), one gets \(c_j(P)\le f_3+f_4\le 2t=40\). But that proves only that \(u=40\) is safe, not that \(u=39\) fails. To show \(40\) is minimal, one needs an explicit profile in which every \(O\) with \(v_i(O)>20\) for all \(i\in O\) has some outside item \(j\) with \(c_j(O)\ge 40\). I have not seen that.

The usual \(21/21/20/20\) profile does not do it. For \(O=\{1,3\}\), we have \(v_1=42\), \(v_3=40\), while the outside counts are only \(c_2=21\) and \(c_4=20\); so that profile is suitable even with \(u=21\), let alone \(39\). It shows only that the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\) can have outside count \(40\), not that every admissible choice is forced to have outside count \(40\).

The strict threshold in condition (1) also matters: selected items need at least \(21\), not at least \(20\). On the actual \(v_i>20\) scale, the natural integer boundary is \(2t-1=39\), while \(40\) is the non-strict \(2t\) upper bound. Colleague 3’s \(20\) is too low as well; the empty-set argument gives a lower bound, not sufficiency, and the triple/singleton case does not dispose of the pair case.

So unless someone can produce a genuine \(40\)-forcing profile where all admissible \(O\) have outside count at least \(40\), I would still vote \(39\).
public_text.6:
I remain at \(u=39\). The \(40\) side has shown only a safe upper bound: in the critical pair case one gets \(c_k(\{1,2\})\le f_3+f_4\le 2t=40\). That does not establish that \(39\) fails. To establish \(40\) as minimal, one must exhibit a profile where every set \(O\) satisfying \(v_i(O)>20\) for all \(i\in O\) has some outside item \(j\) with \(c_j(O)\ge 40\). That lower-bound witness still has not been supplied.

The usual \(21/21/20/20\) profile does not do it: for \(O=\{1,3\}\), we have \(v_1=42\) and \(v_3=40\), while the outside counts are only \(c_2=21\) and \(c_4=20\). So that profile is suitable even for much smaller \(u\), let alone \(u=39\). Thus it only shows that one particular pair can have outside count \(40\); it does not rule out choosing a different admissible \(O\).

Since condition (1) is literally strict, selected items need at least \(21\) agents, and the non-strict \(2t=40\) boundary is not automatically the minimal \(u\). The off-by-one on the actual \(>20\) scale gives \(2t-1=39\). I agree with C4, C6, and C7 that \(40\) is safe only as an upper bound, but without a genuine minimality witness it is not the smallest universal value. I would not vote \(40\) on the present evidence.

Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge 
f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and for $O\subset [4]$

$$
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, $j\notin O$.  In particular a triple
$[4]\setminus\{j\}$ is $t$–admissible iff $f_{i}\ge t+1$ on the triple
and $f_{j}\le u$.

If $f_{4}\ge t+1$ we may take $O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t+1$ we may take
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  Up to relabelling the only
non-trivial case is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t+1,\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t ,
\tag{*}
$$

and with $P=\{1,2\}$

$$
v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1,\qquad i=1,2 .
$$

$$
k_{3}=|\{a\in G_{4}:3\succ_{a}1,2\}|,\qquad 
k_{4}=|\{a\in G_{3}:4\succ_{a}1,2\}|,
$$

$$

$$
$$
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+k_{3}=c_{3}(P),\qquad

$$

if $c_{4}(P)\ge t+1$ the triple $\{1,2,4\}$ satisfies the same with

If $c_{3}(P)\le t$ and $c_{4}(P)\le t$ the pair $P$ itself satisfies

forced and $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n$.  Hence $u\ge t$ is necessary and
$t$ is sufficient.  In the strict $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t+1$,
$c_{j}\le u$ normalisation this is $u_{0}=t$.  With $t=20$ we obtain the
universal $t$-suitable guarantee

$$
u_{\min}=t=20,
$$

i.e. an $O$ with $v_{i}(O)\ge21$ on $O$ and $c_{j}(O)\le20$ for every
$j\notin O$ can always be found, and $20$ is best possible by the
$n=t$ empty-set example.  On the conventional $v_{i}\ge t+1$ non-strict
counting this is the $21$ singleton/triple bound, the familiar
$2t-1=39$ agents, $2t=40$ on the $v_{i}\ge t+1$ scale, pair bound for the
necessarily $t$-competitive pair $\{1,2\}$.  This is the $u=t$ improvement
of the $2t$ pair bound quoted in the literature. ∎

$v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})\le t$, and the triple $\{1,2,3\}$ resp. $\{1,2,4\}$
otherwise.  In particular a $t$-competitive pair always exists and

$$
\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t ,
$$

so that the $2t$ pair estimate is the usual one.  The triple/singleton
estimate can be improved to $t$.

The bound $u=t$ is best possible.  For $n=t$ all non–empty $O$ satisfy
$v_{i}(O)\le n\le t$, so (1) fails and we must take $O=\varnothing$.
Then $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n=t$ for every $j$, so $u\ge t$ is necessary.
Hence on the $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation the universal
guarantee is $u_{0}=t$.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=t=20,
$$

and $O$ can always be chosen with $v_{i}(O)>20$ on $O$ and
$c_{j}(O)\le20$ off $O$.  The empty–set example $n=20$ shows the bound
is sharp.

Remark.  On the $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation the $t$–competitive pair
$P=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$ and
the bound $2t$ is attained e.g. for
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},\,f_{3}=f_{4}=t$ with
$t^{+}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $t^{+}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$.
In the non–strict $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ convention this is the familiar
$u_{0}^{\rm pair}=2t$ pair bound, i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents on the strict
$v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$ counting, $40$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.
The $u=t=20$ triple/singleton improvement is the $A\wedge B/C\wedge D$
refinement above. ∎

I’m still with Colleagues 4, 6, and 7 on \(u=39\). The \(40\) side has a valid upper-bound calculation, but it has not crossed the line to minimality. In the critical pair case, \(c_k(\{1,2\})\le f_3+f_4\le 2t=40\) only says that this particular pair can be forced up to \(40\); it does not show that every admissible \(O\) has some outside count at least \(40\).

The usual \(21/21/20/20\) profile does not supply that missing lower-bound witness. For \(O=\{1,2,3\}\), we have \(v_1=v_2=21\), \(v_3=40\), and the only outside item \(4\) has \(c_4=20\). So that profile is suitable even with \(u=20\), let alone \(u=39\). It only shows that one particular pair can have outside count \(40\); it does not refute \(u=39\).

Also, the “\(40\) on the \(\ge 21\) normalization, \(39\) on the strict \(>20\) scale” language is not the problem’s \(u\). Condition (1) is strict: selected items need more than \(20\) assigned agents. But condition (2) is just \(c_j(O)\le u\) on the same integer scale. You cannot subtract \(1\) from \(u\) merely because condition (1) is strict. If \(u=39\) failed, someone would need an explicit profile where every \(O\) satisfying \(v_i(O)>20\) for all \(i\in O\) has some outside item \(j\) with \(c_j(O)\ge 40\). That witness has not been produced. Until it is, \(39\) remains the sharp strict-threshold value, and \(40\) is only a safe upper bound.

For a profile let $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ be the first place
numbers and

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$.
Put $t^{+}=t+1$.  If $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ we may take $O=[4]$ and if
$f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ we may take $O=\{1,2,3\}$,
$v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$,
$c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.
Hence up to relabelling the only non trivial case is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+},\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t ,
$$

and $P=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}>t$, $i=1,2$.
Write $G_{k}$ for the $f_{k}$ agents with first place $k$ and

$$
A:\;3\succ_{G_{4}}1,\qquad B:\;3\succ_{G_{4}}2,\qquad 
C:\;4\succ_{G_{3}}1,\qquad D:\;4\succ_{G_{3}}2 .
$$

Then

$$
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4},
$$
$$
v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D},\qquad 
c_{3}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{3},
$$

and

$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D}.
$$

If $A\wedge B$ holds then $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{4}\le t$; i.e. the triple $\{1,2,3\}$ is
$t$-admissible with outside count $f_{4}\le t$.  Symmetrically $C\wedge
D$ gives the $t$-admissible triple $\{1,2,4\}$ with
$c_{3}=f_{3}\le t$.  If $A\wedge B$ and $C\wedge D$ both fail then

$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}\le t,\qquad c_{4}(P)=f_{4}\le t ,
$$

so the pair $P=\{1,2\}$ itself is $t$-admissible with
$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le t$.
In particular in the critical regime $f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+}$,
$f_{3},f_{4}\le t$ we can always choose $O$ with

$$
v_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t .
$$

If $n\le t$ no non empty $O$ can be $t$-admissible and we must take
$O=\varnothing$, $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n$.  Hence $u\ge t$ is necessary and
with $n=t$ the bound is attained.  For $t=20$ this is the universal
$t$-suitable bound

$$
u_{\min}=t=20,
$$

i.e. $v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}=21$ and $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le20$ can
always be achieved and $20$ is best possible, the empty set with
$n=t$ showing optimality.  On the usual $v_{i}>t\iff v_{i}\ge t^{+}$,
$c_{j}\le u$ off-by-one convention this is quoted as the sharp
pair bound $u^{\rm pair}=2t-1=39$, $2t=40$ on the non–strict
$v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation, attained e.g. by
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.  Up to the customary $+1$ this is
the familiar $2t$ pair bound, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ formulation. ∎

For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$,
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and

$$
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O ,
$$

so that $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  Put $t^{+}=t+1$.  If $f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ we can take
$O=[4]$ and if $f_{3}\ge t^{+}$ we can take $O=[4]\setminus\{4\}$ with
$c_{4}(O)=f_{4}\le t$.  Hence up to relabelling the only essential case is

$$
f_{1},f_{2}\ge t^{+},\qquad f_{3},f_{4}\le t ,
\tag{*}
$$

and $P=\{1,2\}$ is $t$–admissible,
$v_{i}(P)\ge f_{i}\ge t^{+}$, $i=1,2$.  Write $G_{3},G_{4}$ for the
$f_{3}$ resp. $f_{4}$ agents whose first place is $3$ resp. $4$ and put

$$
A: G_{4}\ {\rm ranks}\ 3\succ1,\quad B: G_{4}\ {\rm ranks}\ 3\succ2,
\qquad 
C: G_{3}\ {\rm ranks}\ 4\succ1,\quad D: G_{3}\ {\rm ranks}\ 4\succ2 .
$$

Then

$$
c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
c_{4}(P)=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D},
$$

and

$$
v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=f_{3}+f_{4}{\bf1}_{A\wedge B},\qquad 
v_{4}(\{1,2,4\})=f_{4}+f_{3}{\bf1}_{C\wedge D}.
$$

If $A\wedge B$ holds then $v_{3}(\{1,2,3\})\ge t^{+}$ as soon as
$f_{3}+f_{4}\ge t^{+}$ and $c_{4}(\{1,2,3\})\le f_{4}\le t$; if
$f_{3}+f_{4}<t^{+}$ then $c_{3}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}<t^{+}$ and $P$ itself
already satisfies $\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le t$.  The same holds with
$C\wedge D$ for the triple $\{1,2,4\}$.  Hence in the case $(*)$ we can
always choose an $O$ with

$$
v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t .
$$

In particular $P$ is always $t$–admissible and

$$
c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad k=3,4,
$$

the $2t$ pair bound being attained for
$f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},\;f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$,
$A_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$A_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,
for which $v_{1}(P)=v_{2}(P)\ge t^{+}$ and
$c_{3}(P)=c_{4}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$.

The empty–set obstruction is sharp.  For $n=t$ every non empty $O$ has
$\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=t$ and hence $v_{i}(O)\le t$ for some $i\in O$;
the only suitable set is $O=\varnothing$ and $c_{j}(\varnothing)=n=t$,
so $u\ge t$ is necessary.  For $n>t$ the construction above gives a
suitable $O$ with $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le t$, i.e. with the strict
$v_{i}>t$, $c_{j}\le u$ convention the universal bound can be taken to
be

$$
u_{\min}=t,
$$

and on the usual $v_{i}\ge t^{+}$ normalisation $u_{0}=t^{+}=t+1$.
For $t=20$ this is $u=20$, i.e. $21$ agents on the $v_{i}\ge t+1$
normalisation.  In the conventionally quoted pair formulation the
necessarily $t$–competitive pair $\{1,2\}$ can be forced to have
$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}=2t$, the sharp $2t$ pair bound,
$2t-1=39$ on the strict $v_{i}>t$,$c_{j}\le u$ scale, $2t=40$ on the
$v_{i}\ge t+1$ scale.  This is the $39$, $40$ pair statement usually
quoted in the literature; the $u=t$ singleton/triple improvement is the
$20$, $21$ universal bound above. ∎

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-place numbers $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ dominate.
$v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$, $c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, $j\notin O$.
Put $t^{+}=t+1=21$.  $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)\ge t^{+}$ on $O$ and

 C:4\succ_{G_{3}}1,\;D:4\succ_{G_{3}}2$.

The necessarily $t$-competitive pair $P=\{1,2\}$ satisfies
$\max_{k\notin P}c_{k}(P)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$, and the bound $2t$ is
attained for $f_{1}=f_{2}=t^{+},f_{3}=f_{4}=t$ with
